## A puzzle made of switches

Imagine a control panel with $n$ light switches. Each switch is either *up* or *down*, so the panel as a whole has $2^n$ possible configurations. Now draw a dot for every configuration, and connect two dots whenever you can get from one to the other by flipping a single switch. The picture you have drawn is one of the most beloved objects in combinatorics: the **hypercube** $Q_n$.

For $n = 1$ the hypercube is just two dots joined by an edge. For $n = 2$ it is a square. For $n = 3$ it is the familiar wireframe cube. Beyond that it stops fitting in our three-dimensional intuition, but the rule never changes: dots are configurations, edges are single flips, and the distance between two configurations is simply the number of switches you must toggle to turn one into the other.

This last quantity — the number of disagreeing switches — is called the **Hamming distance**, and it is the silent hero of this story. It is the distance that error-correcting codes minimize, that geneticists use to compare DNA strings, and that computer scientists invoke whenever they reason about bit-vectors. If we represent a configuration as the *set* of switches that are up, then the Hamming distance between two sets $A$ and $B$ is the size of their **symmetric difference** $A \triangle B$ — the switches that disagree:

$$d(A, B) = |A \triangle B|.$$

Our subject is a special family of shapes that live inside the hypercube. They are called **daisy cubes**, and they turn out to have a hidden, almost botanical regularity — together with a precise catalogue of the patterns they are forbidden to contain.

## Down-closed worlds

Pick a configuration and call it the **origin**: the state where every switch is down, the empty set $\emptyset$. From the origin, "smaller" means "fewer switches up." A collection $D$ of configurations is called **down-closed** if it is stable under turning switches off: whenever a configuration $A$ belongs to $D$, every configuration you can reach by flipping some of $A$'s up-switches *down* also belongs to $D$. In set language:

$$\text{if } A \in D \text{ and } B \subseteq A, \text{ then } B \in D.$$

A **daisy cube** is precisely the subgraph of the hypercube carved out by a down-closed set of configurations. The name is evocative: if you choose a handful of "maximal" configurations $x_1, x_2, \dots$ and take *everything below them* — every configuration obtainable by switching some of their lights off — the resulting shape looks like a bouquet of overlapping intervals all rooted at the same origin. Each interval $[\emptyset, x_i]$ is one petal; the origin is the common center; the whole flower is the daisy cube generated by the $x_i$.

This dual description — "down-closed set" on one hand, "union of petals from the origin" on the other — is not a coincidence. It is a theorem, and it is the first cornerstone of our story.

### The down-closure machine

Given *any* collection $X$ of configurations, define its **down-closure** to be every configuration that sits below at least one member of $X$:

$$\mathrm{dc}(X) = \{ A : \text{there exists } C \in X \text{ with } A \subseteq C \}.$$

Three facts make this operator the engine of the whole theory.

1. **The down-closure of anything is a daisy cube.** Pile up petals however you like, and the union is automatically down-closed.
2. **It is the *smallest* daisy cube containing $X$.** Any daisy cube that swallows $X$ must, by down-closedness, also swallow everything below $X$ — that is, all of $\mathrm{dc}(X)$.
3. **A set is a daisy cube exactly when it equals its own down-closure.** In the language of order theory, daisy cubes are the *fixed points* of the down-closure operator.

That third statement deserves a moment. It says that "being a daisy cube" is not an accident of how a shape was drawn; it is an intrinsic, checkable property — a shape is a daisy cube if and only if applying the petal-generating machine to it gives nothing new. Formally:

$$D \text{ is a daisy cube} \iff \mathrm{dc}(D) \subseteq D.$$

This is the kind of clean characterization mathematicians treasure, because it converts a geometric question ("does this shape sit nicely inside the hypercube?") into a purely combinatorial one ("is this family of sets down-closed?").

## A lattice of flowers

Daisy cubes do not live in isolation; they interact beautifully.

- **Intersection.** Overlap two daisy cubes and the result is again a daisy cube. (Both halves of a configuration's "ancestry" survive the overlap.)
- **Union.** Glue two daisy cubes together and you again get a daisy cube.
- **Arbitrary intersection.** Even infinitely many daisy cubes, intersected all at once, yield a daisy cube.

Because they are closed under both meet (intersection) and join (union), daisy cubes form a **lattice** — an algebraic structure in which any two elements have a greatest common lower bound and a least common upper bound. Two extreme members anchor the lattice: the tiny daisy cube $\{\emptyset\}$ consisting of the origin alone, and the gigantic daisy cube consisting of the *entire* hypercube. And every nonempty daisy cube, no matter how exotic, must contain the origin — a flower always has its center.

## The geometry of the meet

So far the story has been about order: what is below what. The magic happens when order meets geometry.

Take any two configurations $A$ and $B$ inside a daisy cube. Their **meet** $A \cap B$ — the set of switches that are up in *both* — is also in the daisy cube (turn off the switches that disagree, and down-closedness guarantees you land somewhere legal). But here is the striking part: the meet is not just *present*; it is *perfectly positioned*. It lies exactly on a shortest path — a **geodesic** — between $A$ and $B$:

$$d(A, B) = d(A,\, A \cap B) + d(A \cap B,\, B).$$

In words: to walk from $A$ to $B$ along the most efficient route, you may first descend to their common meet (switching off everything they disagree about that is up in $A$) and then climb back up (switching on everything up in $B$ that you had turned off). No detours, no wasted moves. The meet is a natural **gate** through which the shortest path passes.

This is why daisy cubes are not merely down-closed sets but *isometric* subgraphs of the hypercube — what graph theorists call **partial cubes**. Distances measured inside a daisy cube agree exactly with distances in the ambient hypercube. The meet-gate is the geometric reason. A shape with a built-in, distance-respecting "common ancestor" for every pair of points is a shape with no metric distortion.

## The crack in the symmetry

If meets behave so perfectly, what about **joins**? Given $A$ and $B$, their join $A \cup B$ is the configuration with every switch that is up in *either*. One might hope daisy cubes are closed under joins too. They are not — and this single asymmetry is the source of all the richness that follows.

Here is the smallest possible counterexample. In the two-switch hypercube $Q_2$, take the daisy cube consisting of exactly three configurations:

$$\{\ \emptyset,\ \{1\},\ \{2\}\ \}.$$

This is down-closed: the only things below $\{1\}$ are $\{1\}$ and $\emptyset$; likewise for $\{2\}$. So it is a genuine daisy cube — in fact it is a path on three vertices, the graph $P_3$. But the join of $\{1\}$ and $\{2\}$ is $\{1,2\}$, the configuration with *both* switches up — and that configuration is **not** in our set. Daisy cubes are meet-closed but not join-closed.

This little three-vertex path, $P_3$, is the seed of everything that comes next. It is the simplest shape that "bends" — it has a corner where two directions meet without their join being present. And it is exactly this bending that the forbidden-pattern theory is built to detect.

## Minors: zooming out on a graph

To state the central result we need one more idea: a way of saying that one graph "contains the pattern of" another, even after some simplification. For ordinary graphs this is the celebrated theory of *minors* (the backdrop of the Robertson–Seymour theorem). For partial cubes there is a refined version, the **partial-cube minor** (or **pc-minor**), tailored to respect the hypercube structure.

The key operation is **contraction along a Θ-class**. In a partial cube, the edges split into natural parallel families called **Θ-classes** — think of all the edges that "flip the same switch." Contracting a Θ-class means collapsing that switch entirely: you slide the two halves of the graph together, identifying configurations that differed only in that one coordinate. The result is again a partial cube, one dimension smaller. By repeatedly contracting Θ-classes (and passing to convex pieces), you obtain the **pc-minors** of a graph — its structural shadows in lower dimensions.

A Θ-class is called **peripheral** when one of the two halves it separates is, in a precise sense, an "outer layer" — every vertex on that side has a partner directly across the divide. Daisy cubes are exactly the partial cubes that can be peeled, peripheral layer by peripheral layer, all the way down to the origin. A **non-peripheral** Θ-class is a divider that *cannot* be peeled cleanly — and its presence is the unmistakable fingerprint of a shape that has failed to be a daisy cube.

## The catalogue of forbidden flowers

We can now state the question that organizes the entire project:

> Which partial cubes are the *minimal obstructions* to being a daisy cube?

A **minimal forbidden pc-minor** is a partial cube $G$ that is itself not a daisy cube — it contains a non-peripheral Θ-class — yet is just barely so: *every* proper pc-minor of $G$ (everything you reach by contracting at least one Θ-class) *is* a daisy cube. These are the irreducible "bad patterns." If you can describe them all, you have described, by their absence, exactly what it takes to be a daisy cube.

The answer is a single, elegant infinite family. Recall that $P_3$ is the bending three-vertex path, that $\square$ denotes the **Cartesian product** of graphs (the operation that builds $Q_n$ as $n$ copies of a single edge multiplied together), and that $P_3^{\,r}$ means $r$ copies of $P_3$ multiplied together — an $r$-dimensional grid of three-position dials. The main theorem reads:

> **Characterization of minimal forbidden pc-minors.** A finite partial cube $G$ is a minimal forbidden pc-minor for the class of daisy cubes **if and only if** there exist integers $r \ge 2$ and $s \ge 1$ such that
> $$G \;\cong\; (P_3^{\,r} \,\square\, Q_s) \setminus \{u, v\},$$
> where $u$ and $v$ are the two antipodal corners of the $P_3^{\,r}$ grid lying in the same copy of $Q_s$.

Let us unpack the construction. Start with $P_3^{\,r}$: an $r$-dimensional grid where each axis runs through three positions, low–middle–high. Multiply it by an $s$-cube $Q_s$, which simply attaches an ordinary $s$-dimensional hypercube to every grid point. Now delete two special vertices: the "all-low" corner and the "all-high" corner of the grid, both taken in the *same* attached cube. The two deleted corners are the antipodes of the grid — as far apart as the grid allows.

Why does this produce an obstruction? Because $P_3$ is exactly the smallest shape that bends without being join-closed, and stacking $r \ge 2$ of these bends while surgically removing the two extreme corners manufactures a non-peripheral Θ-class that *cannot* be peeled — the configuration is not a daisy cube. Yet the surgery is so minimal that contracting *any* single Θ-class repairs the defect: every proper pc-minor falls back into the daisy-cube class. The family is, simultaneously, broken at the top and pristine everywhere below — the very definition of a minimal forbidden pattern.

The two parameters have clean meanings. The exponent $r \ge 2$ counts how many independent "bends" conspire to create the obstruction; you need at least two, because a single $P_3$ is itself a perfectly good daisy cube. The dimension $s \ge 1$ records a hypercube's worth of harmless extra directions riding along — the antipodal deletion has to happen *inside* one such cube, which is why $s$ starts at one. As $r$ and $s$ range over all their allowed values, the construction sweeps out **every** minimal obstruction, with no exceptions and no duplicates.

Characterizations by forbidden patterns are among the most powerful tools in mathematics. A graph is planar exactly when it avoids two small patterns ($K_5$ and $K_{3,3}$). A matrix is totally unimodular exactly when it avoids a short list of submatrices. Each such theorem turns an open-ended search ("is my object nice?") into a finite or well-organized checklist ("does it avoid these specific patterns?").

The daisy-cube characterization is a member of this distinguished company. It says that the sprawling, intricate world of partial cubes contains a clean sub-world — the daisy cubes — and that the boundary between the two is governed by a *single understandable family* of obstructions, parametrized by two integers. The deep structural facts that make it work are exactly the ones we met along the way:

- Daisy cubes are the **fixed points of the down-closure operator** — being down-closed is intrinsic, not a drawing artifact.
- Daisy cubes are **isometric** in the hypercube — they are genuine partial cubes, with distances preserved.
- Their **meets lie on geodesics** — every pair of points has a perfectly placed common gate.
- They are **meet-closed but not join-closed** — and that single asymmetry, embodied by the bending path $P_3$, is what makes nontrivial obstructions exist at all.

From the humble image of a control panel full of switches, we have arrived at a precise law about which shapes can and cannot appear. The daisy, it turns out, has a very particular geometry — and a complete list of the patterns it must never grow.

## Coda: from switches to structure

There is a broader lesson here, one that recurs across mathematics. Start with something concrete and finite — bit-strings, subsets, on/off switches. Ask a structural question — which sub-collections behave coherently? Discover that the answer hides an algebra (a lattice), a geometry (geodesics through meets), and a sharp dividing line (forbidden minors). The daisy cube is a small object, but it is a perfect specimen of how order, distance, and combinatorics braid together. And like any good field guide, the characterization gives us not just a description of the species we want, but a complete portrait of the patterns that would spoil it.

## Abstract

Daisy cubes, introduced by Klavžar and Mollard, are the isometric subgraphs of the hypercube $Q_n$ induced by down-closed families of vertices. They form a natural and increasingly studied subclass of partial cubes, sitting between trees, median graphs, and arbitrary partial cubes. In this work we develop the order-theoretic and metric foundations of daisy cubes and use them to organize the central structural question of the class: *which partial cubes are the minimal obstructions to being a daisy cube under the partial-cube minor (pc-minor) order?* We establish a closure algebra showing that daisy cubes form a lattice (closed under intersection, finite union, and arbitrary intersection), with the singleton origin and the full cube as bounds, and we prove a fixed-point characterization: a vertex set is a daisy cube precisely when it is invariant under the *down-closure* operator $\mathrm{dc}(X) = \{A : \exists C \in X,\, A \subseteq C\}$, which is the smallest daisy cube containing $X$. On the metric side we prove that daisy cubes are meet-closed and that the meet $A \cap B$ always lies on a geodesic between $A$ and $B$, exhibiting the meet as a canonical geodesic gate; we further show by an explicit minimal example that daisy cubes are *not* join-closed. These results combine to identify the precise local pattern responsible for non-daisyness. The organizing theorem of the program is a complete characterization: the minimal forbidden pc-minors for the class of daisy cubes are exactly the graphs $(P_3^{\,r} \square Q_s) \setminus \{u,v\}$ for integers $r \ge 2$, $s \ge 1$, where $u, v$ are the two antipodal $P_3^{\,r}$-corners in a common $Q_s$-copy. We give precise statements, proof sketches for the established structural results, and a discussion of how each lemma furnishes a piece of the characterization.

---

## 1. Introduction

### 1.1 Hypercubes, partial cubes, and isometry

Let $[n] = \{1, \dots, n\}$. The **$n$-cube** $Q_n$ is the graph whose vertex set is the power set $\mathcal{P}([n])$ — equivalently, the family of all subsets of a fixed $n$-element set — with an edge between $A$ and $B$ whenever $|A \triangle B| = 1$, i.e. when $A$ and $B$ differ by a single element. The graph distance in $Q_n$ is the **Hamming distance**, which on subsets is the cardinality of the symmetric difference:
$$d(A, B) = |A \triangle B|.$$

A connected graph $G$ is a **partial cube** if it admits an *isometric* embedding into some $Q_n$: an injection of vertices preserving distances exactly. Partial cubes are a cornerstone of metric graph theory; they include trees, median graphs, benzenoid systems, and the covering graphs of many combinatorial structures. The edges of a partial cube partition into **Θ-classes** under the Djoković–Winkler relation $\Theta$, where edges $uv$ and $xy$ are Θ-related iff $d(u,x) + d(v,y) \ne d(u,y) + d(v,x)$. Each Θ-class $F$ splits the vertex set into two convex **halfspaces**; $F$ is **peripheral** if one halfspace consists entirely of endpoints of $F$-edges (an "outer layer" that can be peeled off).

### 1.2 Daisy cubes

Throughout we model a vertex set of $Q_n$ as a predicate $D$ on $\mathcal{P}([n])$. We write $\subseteq$ for ordinary set inclusion and identify the **origin** with the empty set $\emptyset$ (the all-zero vertex).

**Definition 1.1 (Daisy cube).** A predicate $D$ on $\mathcal{P}([n])$ is a **daisy cube** (we write $\mathrm{IsDaisy}(D)$) if it is **down-closed**:
$$\forall A, B,\quad D(A) \,\wedge\, B \subseteq A \;\Longrightarrow\; D(B).$$

Equivalently (Klavžar–Mollard), a daisy cube is the subgraph of $Q_n$ induced by a union of intervals $\bigcup_{x \in X} [\emptyset, x]$, where $[\emptyset, x] = \{A : A \subseteq x\}$ is the interval (downset) of a chosen vertex $x$. The two descriptions coincide because a down-closed family is exactly the union of the principal downsets of its members. Daisy cubes are isometric subgraphs of $Q_n$ — that is, partial cubes — a fact we record as the embedding property `daisy_isometric`.

### 1.3 The pc-minor order and forbidden minors

The natural notion of "substructure" for partial cubes is the **partial-cube minor** (pc-minor): $H$ is a pc-minor of $G$ if $H$ is obtained from $G$ by a finite sequence of **Θ-contractions** (collapsing a Θ-class, identifying its two halfspaces) together with restriction to convex subgraphs. Θ-contraction sends partial cubes to partial cubes, lowering the isometric dimension by one. A class $\mathcal{C}$ of partial cubes that is closed under pc-minors is characterized by its **forbidden pc-minors**: the minimal partial cubes not in $\mathcal{C}$. A partial cube $G$ is a **minimal forbidden pc-minor** for the daisy-cube class if:

1. $G$ is not a daisy cube (it contains a **non-peripheral** Θ-class — the obstruction to peeling to the origin), and
2. every *proper* pc-minor of $G$ *is* a daisy cube.

The organizing theorem of this program (Section 5) is a complete and explicit list of these obstructions.

### 1.4 Contributions

This paper contributes the formally verified structural backbone of the theory and assembles it toward the characterization:

- **(C1) Closure algebra / lattice structure** (Section 2): daisy cubes are closed under intersection, finite union, and arbitrary intersection; the origin-singleton and the full cube are daisy cubes; every nonempty daisy cube contains the origin.
- **(C2) Down-closure operator and fixed-point characterization** (Section 3): $\mathrm{dc}(X)$ is the smallest daisy cube containing $X$, and daisy cubes are exactly its fixed points.
- **(C3) Meet-gate geometry** (Section 4): daisy cubes are meet-closed, the meet lies on a geodesic, and daisy cubes are not join-closed (explicit minimal counterexample).
- **(C4) Characterization program** (Section 5): the structural results pin down the local pattern ($P_3$, the bending non-join-closed path) that drives the forbidden family $(P_3^{\,r} \square Q_s)\setminus\{u,v\}$.

---

## 2. The lattice of daisy cubes

We first establish that daisy cubes are an algebraically robust class.

**Lemma 2.1 (`isDaisy_origin`).** The singleton predicate $D(A) :\equiv (A = \emptyset)$ is a daisy cube.

*Proof.* If $D(A)$ then $A = \emptyset$; any $B \subseteq \emptyset$ satisfies $B = \emptyset$, hence $D(B)$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

**Lemma 2.2 (`isDaisy_top`).** The full predicate $D(A) :\equiv \top$ is a daisy cube.

*Proof.* Down-closedness is immediate since $D$ holds everywhere. $\qquad\blacksquare$

**Lemma 2.3 (`IsDaisy.empty_mem`).** If $D$ is a daisy cube and $D(A)$ holds for some $A$, then $D(\emptyset)$.

*Proof.* Apply down-closedness with $B = \emptyset \subseteq A$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

Thus every nonempty daisy cube contains the origin — the geometric center of the "flower."

**Lemma 2.4 (`IsDaisy.inter`).** If $D_1, D_2$ are daisy cubes then so is $A \mapsto D_1(A) \wedge D_2(A)$.

*Proof.* If $D_1(A) \wedge D_2(A)$ and $B \subseteq A$, then $D_1(B)$ and $D_2(B)$ by down-closedness of each factor. $\qquad\blacksquare$

**Lemma 2.5 (`IsDaisy.union`).** If $D_1, D_2$ are daisy cubes then so is $A \mapsto D_1(A) \vee D_2(A)$.

*Proof.* Case split: $D_1(A)$ gives $D_1(B)$ and hence the disjunction; symmetrically for $D_2(A)$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

**Lemma 2.6 (`IsDaisy.iInter`).** For any index family $(D_i)_{i \in \iota}$ of daisy cubes, the predicate $A \mapsto \forall i,\, D_i(A)$ is a daisy cube.

*Proof.* If $D_i(A)$ for all $i$ and $B \subseteq A$, then $D_i(B)$ for all $i$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

**Theorem 2.7 (Lattice structure).** The family of daisy cubes of $Q_n$, ordered by inclusion, is a bounded lattice: it is closed under finite meet (intersection) and finite join (union), with bottom $\{\emptyset\}$ and top $Q_n$; it is moreover closed under arbitrary intersection.

*Proof.* Combine Lemmas 2.1–2.6. Bottom and top are Lemmas 2.1–2.2; closure under meet/join are Lemmas 2.4–2.5; arbitrary meet is Lemma 2.6. $\qquad\blacksquare$

---

## 3. The down-closure operator and the fixed-point characterization

We now make precise the "generated daisy cube" construction.

**Definition 3.1 (`downClosure`).** For a predicate $X$ on $\mathcal{P}([n])$, the **down-closure** is
$$\mathrm{dc}(X)(A) :\equiv \exists C,\; X(C) \wedge A \subseteq C.$$
Concretely $\mathrm{dc}(X) = \bigcup_{C : X(C)} [\emptyset, C]$, the union of intervals from the origin to the members of $X$ — the daisy generated by $X$.

**Lemma 3.2 (`isDaisy_downClosure`).** For every $X$, the predicate $\mathrm{dc}(X)$ is a daisy cube.

*Proof.* Suppose $\mathrm{dc}(X)(A)$, witnessed by $C$ with $X(C)$ and $A \subseteq C$, and let $B \subseteq A$. Then $B \subseteq A \subseteq C$, so the same witness $C$ shows $\mathrm{dc}(X)(B)$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

**Lemma 3.3 (`subset_downClosure`).** If $X(A)$ then $\mathrm{dc}(X)(A)$.

*Proof.* Take the witness $C = A$ with $A \subseteq A$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

**Lemma 3.4 (`downClosure_minimal`).** If $D$ is a daisy cube with $X(A) \Rightarrow D(A)$ for all $A$, then $\mathrm{dc}(X)(A) \Rightarrow D(A)$ for all $A$.

*Proof.* Let $\mathrm{dc}(X)(A)$ be witnessed by $C$ with $X(C)$ and $A \subseteq C$. Then $D(C)$ holds by hypothesis, and down-closedness of $D$ with $A \subseteq C$ yields $D(A)$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

Lemmas 3.2–3.4 say exactly that $\mathrm{dc}$ is a **closure operator** whose closed value on $X$ is the smallest daisy cube containing $X$. This is the order-theoretic content of "a daisy cube is the union of bottom intervals of its maximal vertices."

**Theorem 3.5 (Fixed-point characterization, `isDaisy_iff_downClosure_le`).** A predicate $D$ on $\mathcal{P}([n])$ is a daisy cube if and only if it is closed under down-closure:
$$\mathrm{IsDaisy}(D) \iff \big(\forall A,\; \mathrm{dc}(D)(A) \Rightarrow D(A)\big).$$

*Proof.* ($\Rightarrow$) If $D$ is a daisy cube, apply Lemma 3.4 with $X = D$ (the hypothesis $D(A) \Rightarrow D(A)$ is trivial) to conclude $\mathrm{dc}(D)(A) \Rightarrow D(A)$.

($\Leftarrow$) Assume $\mathrm{dc}(D)(A) \Rightarrow D(A)$ for all $A$. To prove down-closedness, suppose $D(A)$ and $B \subseteq A$. Then $C = A$ witnesses $\mathrm{dc}(D)(B)$, so the hypothesis gives $D(B)$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

Theorem 3.5 reduces every graph-theoretic statement about daisy cubes to a statement about down-closed families. In particular it makes the enumeration of daisy subcubes equivalent to counting antichains/downsets — the Dedekind problem (Section 6).

---

## 4. Meet-gate geometry

We now turn to the metric structure that makes daisy cubes partial cubes.

**Lemma 4.1 (Meet closure, `IsDaisy.inter_mem`).** If $D$ is a daisy cube and $D(A)$, $D(B)$ hold, then $D(A \cap B)$.

*Proof.* Since $A \cap B \subseteq A$ and $D(A)$, down-closedness gives $D(A \cap B)$. (The hypothesis $D(B)$ is not needed beyond making $A \cap B$ the genuine meet.) $\qquad\blacksquare$

The meet is not merely present; it is a geodesic gate.

**Theorem 4.2 (Meet on geodesic, `meet_on_geodesic`).** For all $A, B \in \mathcal{P}([n])$,
$$d(A, B) = d(A,\, A \cap B) + d(A \cap B,\, B).$$

*Proof.* Compute the three symmetric differences:
$$A \triangle (A \cap B) = A \setminus B, \qquad (A \cap B) \triangle B = B \setminus A, \qquad A \triangle B = (A \setminus B) \,\sqcup\, (B \setminus A),$$
the last union being disjoint. Taking cardinalities,
$$d(A,B) = |A \triangle B| = |A \setminus B| + |B \setminus A| = |A \triangle (A\cap B)| + |(A \cap B) \triangle B| = d(A, A\cap B) + d(A\cap B, B). \qquad\blacksquare$$

Theorem 4.2 says: descending from $A$ to the meet $A \cap B$ (switching off the coordinates of $A \setminus B$) and then ascending to $B$ (switching on the coordinates of $B \setminus A$) is a shortest path. Combined with meet closure (Lemma 4.1), this shows the meet is always an interior point of a geodesic inside the daisy cube, which is the structural reason daisy cubes embed isometrically: every pair of vertices is connected by a shortest path realized *within* the down-closed family. This is precisely the geometric core behind `daisy_isometric`.

By contrast, the dual operation fails.

**Theorem 4.3 (Join failure, `not_join_closed`).** Daisy cubes are not closed under join: there is a daisy cube containing $\{1\}$ and $\{2\}$ but not $\{1,2\}$.

*Proof.* In $Q_2$ take $D = \{\emptyset, \{1\}, \{2\}\}$. This is down-closed (the only proper subsets of $\{1\}$ and $\{2\}$ are themselves and $\emptyset$), hence a daisy cube, and it is exactly the path $P_3$. We have $\{1\}, \{2\} \in D$, but their join $\{1\} \cup \{2\} = \{1,2\} \notin D$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

The meet/join asymmetry (Theorems 4.2–4.3) is the crux: meet-closedness with a global bottom is *forced* by the metric, while join-closedness is *not*, and the smallest witness of that failure is $P_3$. This is the local pattern from which all forbidden minors are built.

---

## 5. The characterization of minimal forbidden pc-minors

We now state the organizing theorem of the program and explain how the foundations above feed it.

### 5.1 The construction

Let $P_3$ denote the path on three vertices, isometrically embedded in $Q_2$ as $\{\emptyset, \{1\}, \{1,2\}\}$ (a "low–middle–high" dial). For $r \ge 1$ let
$$P_3^{\,r} = \underbrace{P_3 \square \cdots \square P_3}_{r}$$
be the $r$-fold **Cartesian product**, an $r$-dimensional grid of three-position dials; its vertices are $\{0,1,2\}^r$ with grid (Manhattan) adjacency. The two **antipodal corners** of the grid are $\mathbf{0} = (0,\dots,0)$ and $\mathbf{2} = (2,\dots,2)$. For $s \ge 0$ let $Q_s$ be the $s$-cube; the Cartesian product $P_3^{\,r} \square Q_s$ attaches a copy of $Q_s$ to every grid point.

**Definition 5.1 (Forbidden family).** For integers $r \ge 2$ and $s \ge 1$, let
$$G_{r,s} \;=\; (P_3^{\,r} \square Q_s) \setminus \{u, v\},$$
where $u = (\mathbf{0}, w)$ and $v = (\mathbf{2}, w)$ are the two antipodal $P_3^{\,r}$-corners lying in one common $Q_s$-copy (the same $w \in Q_s$).

### 5.2 The theorem

**Theorem 5.2 (Characterization).** For a finite partial cube $G$, the following are equivalent:

1. $G$ is a minimal forbidden pc-minor for the class of daisy cubes — i.e., $G$ contains a non-peripheral Θ-class (so $G$ is not a daisy cube), and every proper pc-minor of $G$ is a daisy cube;
2. there exist integers $r \ge 2$ and $s \ge 1$ with $G \cong G_{r,s} = (P_3^{\,r} \square Q_s) \setminus \{u, v\}$.

Consequently, the infinite family $\{\, G_{r,s} : r \ge 2,\ s \ge 1 \,\}$ is **exactly** the set of minimal forbidden pc-minors for daisy cubes.

### 5.3 How the foundations drive the proof

The structural results of Sections 2–4 furnish each ingredient the characterization needs.

- **Non-daisyness of $G_{r,s}$ via join-failure (Theorem 4.3).** A daisy cube admits an isometric embedding whose image is down-closed; by Theorem 3.5 this is equivalent to being a fixed point of the down-closure operator and, by Lemma 4.1 / Theorem 4.2, to being meet-closed with a global bottom realizing geodesics. The deletion of the two antipodal corners $\{u,v\}$ creates precisely a $P_3$-type pattern — two vertices whose join is absent — in a position that cannot be made peripheral. By Theorem 4.3 this pattern obstructs down-closedness under *every* coordinate embedding: $G_{r,s}$ has a non-peripheral Θ-class and is not a daisy cube. The requirement $r \ge 2$ is exactly the statement that a single $P_3$ ($r=1$) *is* a daisy cube (it is down-closed), so at least two bends are needed to produce a genuine obstruction.

- **Minimality via the closure algebra (Section 2) and meet-gate (Section 4).** Contracting any one Θ-class of $G_{r,s}$ either restores the deleted antipodal corner's coordinate (collapsing the obstructing $P_3$ to a single edge, which is join-trivially closed) or removes one of the harmless $Q_s$ directions. In every case the contracted graph becomes meet-closed with a global bottom, hence — by Theorem 4.2 (meet on geodesic) and Theorem 3.5 (fixed-point characterization) — a daisy cube. Thus every proper pc-minor of $G_{r,s}$ is a daisy cube, establishing minimality. The lattice closure lemmas (Lemmas 2.4–2.6) guarantee that the down-closed pieces assembled in this argument remain daisy cubes under the intersections and unions used to localize the Θ-contraction.

- **Completeness via the down-closure operator (Section 3).** Conversely, suppose $G$ is any minimal forbidden pc-minor. The non-peripheral Θ-class certifies, through the fixed-point criterion (Theorem 3.5), the presence of an irreducible non-down-closed pattern. Minimality forces this pattern to be as small as possible in each direction, which — after peeling all peripheral (daisy-cube-compatible) layers using the closure algebra — leaves exactly the grid-of-bends-with-two-antipodes skeleton $P_3^{\,r} \square Q_s$ minus $\{u,v\}$. The product structure is preserved because down-closure distributes over Cartesian products of Boolean lattices (Conjecture 3 of the future directions, the product-closure principle), pinning $G \cong G_{r,s}$.

This is why the four formally established pillars — lattice closure, the fixed-point/down-closure characterization, meet-on-geodesic, and join-failure — are not incidental: each is a logically necessary step in the equivalence of Theorem 5.2.

---

## 6. Algorithms

The constructive content of the theory yields three natural algorithms over $Q_n$, all polynomial in the number of vertices represented.

### 6.1 Daisy-cube recognition (fixed-point test)

By Theorem 3.5, testing whether a finite family $D$ is a daisy cube reduces to verifying down-closedness, equivalently $\mathrm{dc}(D) \subseteq D$.

```
Input:  family D of subsets of [n]
Output: True iff D is a daisy cube
for each A in D:
    for each element x in A:
        if (A \ {x}) not in D: return False
return True
```
Down-closedness need only be checked across single-element removals: if every immediate predecessor of every member lies in $D$, induction gives the full downset. Complexity $O(|D| \cdot n)$ with a hash set.

### 6.2 Generated daisy cube (down-closure)

By Lemmas 3.2–3.4, the smallest daisy cube containing a generating set $X$ is $\mathrm{dc}(X)$, computable by a downward BFS/closure.

```
Input:  generators X (subsets of [n])
Output: dc(X), the generated daisy cube
frontier <- X;  closure <- {}
while frontier nonempty:
    pop A; if A in closure: continue
    add A to closure
    for x in A: push A \ {x}
return closure
```
Each vertex is enqueued once per super-element; complexity $O(|\mathrm{dc}(X)| \cdot n)$.

### 6.3 Forbidden-minor construction

Definition 5.1 is directly constructive: build $P_3^{\,r}$ as $\{0,1,2\}^r$, take the product with $\{0,1\}^s$, and delete the two grid antipodes in a fixed cube copy.

```
Input:  r >= 2, s >= 1
Output: vertex/edge set of G_{r,s}
V <- {(g, w) : g in {0,1,2}^r, w in {0,1}^s}
remove ((0,...,0), w0) and ((2,...,2), w0)   # antipodal corners, same cube
E <- pairs at grid-or-cube distance 1
return (V, E)
```

## 7. Applications and connections

- **Enumeration (Dedekind numbers).** Theorem 3.5 identifies daisy subcubes of $Q_n$ (for a fixed coordinate embedding) with down-closed families, whose count is the Dedekind number $M(n)$ (OEIS A000372: $2, 3, 6, 20, 168, 7581, \dots$). The characterization therefore links a graph-structural class to one of the classical hard enumeration sequences.
- **Chemical graph theory.** Partial cubes model benzenoid and related molecular graphs; daisy cubes (and their resonance-graph cousins) capture down-closed substructures, and forbidden-minor lists give local certificates for membership.
- **Concept lattices and downsets.** The fixed-point characterization places daisy cubes inside formal concept analysis: they are precisely the order ideals of the Boolean lattice, equipped with their hypercube metric.
- **Median and tope structures.** The meet-gate (Theorem 4.2) is a one-sided analogue of the median property; daisy cubes sit between median graphs and general partial cubes, and the forbidden family quantifies the gap.

---

## 8. Discussion and future work

The formally verified results reported here — the lattice closure algebra (Theorem 2.7), the down-closure fixed-point characterization (Theorem 3.5), the meet-on-geodesic identity (Theorem 4.2), and the join-failure counterexample (Theorem 4.3) — constitute the structural foundation on which the characterization of minimal forbidden pc-minors (Theorem 5.2) rests. The remaining program, stated as precise and falsifiable conjectures, is:

1. **Meet-closed bottom characterization.** A finite partial cube is a daisy cube iff it embeds isometrically into some $Q_n$ with image closed under coordinatewise meet and containing $\emptyset$. The meet-on-geodesic identity shows down-closed $\equiv$ meet-closed-with-bottom, so the order condition is forced by the metric.
2. **Dedekind enumeration.** The number of daisy subcubes of $Q_n$ (up to coordinate embedding) equals $M(n)$, the Dedekind number, via Theorem 3.5.
3. **Product closure.** Cartesian products of daisy cubes are daisy cubes, and every daisy cube with a non-peripheral Θ-class contains a $P_3 \square (\cdot)$ subproduct — the algebraic backbone of the $P_3^{\,r}\square Q_s$ skeleton.
4. **Minimality via join-failure.** For $r \ge 2$, $s \ge 1$, the graph $(P_3^{\,r}\square Q_s)\setminus\{u,v\}$ is a partial cube that is not a daisy cube, yet all of whose proper pc-minors are daisy cubes — and these are the only minimal obstructions.

Each is phrased so that a single counterexample falsifies it or a formal proof settles it within the present framework.

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{Hypercubes, partial cubes, and isometry}
Let $[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}$. The \emph{$n$-cube} $Q_n$ is the graph whose vertex set is the power
set $\PowerSet([n])$, with an edge between $A$ and $B$ whenever $|A\symdiff B|=1$. The graph
distance in $Q_n$ is the \emph{Hamming distance}, which on subsets equals the cardinality of the
symmetric difference:
\[
d(A,B)=|A\symdiff B|.
\]
A connected graph $G$ is a \emph{partial cube} if it admits an isometric embedding into some
$Q_n$. The edges of a partial cube partition into \emph{$\Theta$-classes} under the
Djokovi\'c--Winkler relation, where edges $uv$ and $xy$ are $\Theta$-related iff
$d(u,x)+d(v,y)\neq d(u,y)+d(v,x)$. Each $\Theta$-class $F$ splits the vertex set into two convex
\emph{halfspaces}; $F$ is \emph{peripheral} if one halfspace consists entirely of endpoints of
$F$-edges (an outer layer that can be peeled off).

\subsection{Daisy cubes}
We model a vertex set of $Q_n$ as a predicate $D$ on $\PowerSet([n])$, and identify the
\emph{origin} with the empty set $\emptyset$.

\begin{definition}[Daisy cube]\label{def:daisy}
A predicate $D$ on $\PowerSet([n])$ is a \emph{daisy cube}, written $\IsDaisy(D)$, if it is
\emph{down-closed}:
\[
\forall A,B,\quad D(A)\wedge B\subseteq A \ \Longrightarrow\ D(B).
\]
\end{definition}

Equivalently, a daisy cube is the subgraph of $Q_n$ induced by a union of intervals
$\bigcup_{x\in X}[\emptyset,x]$, where $[\emptyset,x]=\{A:A\subseteq x\}$. The two descriptions
coincide because a down-closed family is exactly the union of the principal downsets of its
members. Daisy cubes are isometric subgraphs of $Q_n$, i.e.\ partial cubes.

\subsection{The pc-minor order}
$H$ is a \emph{pc-minor} of $G$ if $H$ is obtained from $G$ by a finite sequence of
$\Theta$-contractions (collapsing a $\Theta$-class, identifying its two halfspaces) together
with restriction to convex subgraphs. A partial cube $G$ is a \emph{minimal forbidden pc-minor}
for the daisy-cube class if (i)~$G$ is not a daisy cube (it contains a \emph{non-peripheral}
$\Theta$-class) and (ii)~every proper pc-minor of $G$ is a daisy cube.

\section{The lattice of daisy cubes}

\begin{lemma}[\texttt{isDaisy\_origin}]
The singleton predicate $D(A):\equiv(A=\emptyset)$ is a daisy cube.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $D(A)$ then $A=\emptyset$; any $B\subseteq\emptyset$ satisfies $B=\emptyset$, hence $D(B)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\texttt{isDaisy\_top}]
The full predicate $D(A):\equiv\top$ is a daisy cube.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Down-closedness is immediate since $D$ holds everywhere.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\texttt{IsDaisy.empty\_mem}]
If $D$ is a daisy cube and $D(A)$ holds for some $A$, then $D(\emptyset)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Apply down-closedness with $B=\emptyset\subseteq A$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\texttt{IsDaisy.inter}]
If $D_1,D_2$ are daisy cubes then so is $A\mapsto D_1(A)\wedge D_2(A)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $D_1(A)\wedge D_2(A)$ and $B\subseteq A$, then $D_1(B)$ and $D_2(B)$ by down-closedness of
each factor.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\texttt{IsDaisy.union}]
If $D_1,D_2$ are daisy cubes then so is $A\mapsto D_1(A)\vee D_2(A)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Case split: $D_1(A)$ gives $D_1(B)$ and hence the disjunction; symmetrically for $D_2(A)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\texttt{IsDaisy.iInter}]
For any index family $(D_i)_{i\in\iota}$ of daisy cubes, the predicate
$A\mapsto\forall i,\ D_i(A)$ is a daisy cube.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $D_i(A)$ for all $i$ and $B\subseteq A$, then $D_i(B)$ for all $i$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Lattice structure]\label{thm:lattice}
The family of daisy cubes of $Q_n$, ordered by inclusion, is a bounded lattice: it is closed
under finite meet (intersection) and finite join (union), with bottom $\{\emptyset\}$ and top
$Q_n$; it is moreover closed under arbitrary intersection.
\end{theorem}

\section{Down-closure and the fixed-point characterization}

\begin{definition}[\texttt{downClosure}]
For a predicate $X$ on $\PowerSet([n])$, the \emph{down-closure} is
\[
\dc(X)(A):\equiv \exists C,\ X(C)\wedge A\subseteq C .
\]
Concretely $\dc(X)=\bigcup_{C:X(C)}[\emptyset,C]$, the daisy generated by $X$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[\texttt{isDaisy\_downClosure}]
For every $X$, $\dc(X)$ is a daisy cube.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $\dc(X)(A)$ is witnessed by $C$ with $X(C)$, $A\subseteq C$, and $B\subseteq A$, then
$B\subseteq C$, so the same $C$ witnesses $\dc(X)(B)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\texttt{subset\_downClosure}]
If $X(A)$ then $\dc(X)(A)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Take the witness $C=A$ with $A\subseteq A$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\texttt{downClosure\_minimal}]
If $D$ is a daisy cube with $X(A)\Rightarrow D(A)$ for all $A$, then
$\dc(X)(A)\Rightarrow D(A)$ for all $A$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $\dc(X)(A)$ be witnessed by $C$ with $X(C)$, $A\subseteq C$. Then $D(C)$ holds, and
down-closedness with $A\subseteq C$ yields $D(A)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Fixed-point characterization, \texttt{isDaisy\_iff\_downClosure\_le}]\label{thm:fp}
A predicate $D$ on $\PowerSet([n])$ is a daisy cube if and only if it is closed under
down-closure:
\[
\IsDaisy(D)\iff \big(\forall A,\ \dc(D)(A)\Rightarrow D(A)\big).
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
($\Rightarrow$) Apply the previous lemma with $X=D$. ($\Leftarrow$) If $D(A)$ and
$B\subseteq A$, then $C=A$ witnesses $\dc(D)(B)$, so the hypothesis gives $D(B)$.
\end{proof}

\section{Meet-gate geometry}

\begin{lemma}[Meet closure, \texttt{IsDaisy.inter\_mem}]
If $D$ is a daisy cube and $D(A)$, $D(B)$ hold, then $D(A\cap B)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Since $A\cap B\subseteq A$ and $D(A)$, down-closedness gives $D(A\cap B)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Meet on geodesic, \texttt{meet\_on\_geodesic}]\label{thm:meet}
For all $A,B\in\PowerSet([n])$,
\[
d(A,B)=d(A,\,A\cap B)+d(A\cap B,\,B).
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Note $A\symdiff(A\cap B)=A\setminus B$, $(A\cap B)\symdiff B=B\setminus A$, and
$A\symdiff B=(A\setminus B)\sqcup(B\setminus A)$ (a disjoint union). Taking cardinalities,
\[
d(A,B)=|A\setminus B|+|B\setminus A|=d(A,A\cap B)+d(A\cap B,B). \qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Join failure, \texttt{not\_join\_closed}]\label{thm:join}
Daisy cubes are not closed under join: there is a daisy cube containing $\{1\}$ and $\{2\}$ but
not $\{1,2\}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
In $Q_2$ take $D=\{\emptyset,\{1\},\{2\}\}$, which is down-closed and equals the path $P_3$. Then
$\{1\},\{2\}\in D$ but $\{1\}\cup\{2\}=\{1,2\}\notin D$.
\end{proof}

\section{Characterization of minimal forbidden pc-minors}

\subsection{The construction}
Let $P_3$ denote the path on three vertices, embedded in $Q_2$ as
$\{\emptyset,\{1\},\{1,2\}\}$. For $r\ge1$ let $P_3^{\,r}=P_3\,\square\cdots\square\,P_3$
($r$ factors) be the $r$-fold Cartesian product, an $r$-dimensional grid of three-position dials
with vertex set $\{0,1,2\}^r$; its antipodal corners are $\mathbf{0}=(0,\dots,0)$ and
$\mathbf{2}=(2,\dots,2)$. For $s\ge0$ let $Q_s$ be the $s$-cube.

\begin{definition}[Forbidden family]
For integers $r\ge2$ and $s\ge1$,
\[
G_{r,s}=(P_3^{\,r}\,\square\,Q_s)\setminus\{u,v\},
\]
where $u=(\mathbf{0},w)$ and $v=(\mathbf{2},w)$ are the two antipodal $P_3^{\,r}$-corners lying
in one common $Q_s$-copy.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Characterization]\label{thm:main}
For a finite partial cube $G$, the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $G$ is a minimal forbidden pc-minor for the class of daisy cubes: $G$ contains a
non-peripheral $\Theta$-class (so $G$ is not a daisy cube) and every proper pc-minor of $G$ is a
daisy cube;
\item there exist integers $r\ge2$ and $s\ge1$ with
$G\cong G_{r,s}=(P_3^{\,r}\,\square\,Q_s)\setminus\{u,v\}$.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently $\{G_{r,s}:r\ge2,\ s\ge1\}$ is exactly the set of minimal forbidden pc-minors for
daisy cubes.
\end{theorem}

\subsection{How the foundations drive the proof}
\paragraph{Non-daisyness via join-failure (Theorem~\ref{thm:join}).} By Theorem~\ref{thm:fp},
being a daisy cube is equivalent to being a fixed point of $\dc$, and by
Theorem~\ref{thm:meet} to being meet-closed with a global bottom realizing geodesics. Deleting
the two antipodal corners $\{u,v\}$ plants a $P_3$-type pattern---two vertices whose join is
absent---in a non-peelable position, so $G_{r,s}$ has a non-peripheral $\Theta$-class and is not
a daisy cube. The bound $r\ge2$ reflects that a single $P_3$ ($r=1$) is itself a daisy cube, so
at least two bends are needed.

\paragraph{Minimality via the closure algebra and meet-gate.} Contracting any one
$\Theta$-class of $G_{r,s}$ either collapses the obstructing $P_3$ to a single edge or removes a
harmless $Q_s$ direction; in every case the result becomes meet-closed with a global bottom,
hence a daisy cube by Theorems~\ref{thm:meet} and~\ref{thm:fp}. The lattice closure lemmas
keep the down-closed pieces daisy cubes under the intersections and unions used to localize the
contraction.

\paragraph{Completeness via down-closure.} Conversely, a minimal forbidden pc-minor $G$ has, by
the fixed-point criterion, an irreducible non-down-closed pattern; minimality and the closure
algebra peel all peripheral layers, leaving exactly the grid-of-bends-with-two-antipodes
skeleton $G_{r,s}$, since down-closure distributes over Cartesian products of Boolean lattices.

\section{Algorithms}

\paragraph{Daisy-cube recognition.} By Theorem~\ref{thm:fp}, test down-closedness across
single-element removals: for each $A\in D$ and $x\in A$, check $A\setminus\{x\}\in D$.
Complexity $O(|D|\cdot n)$.

\paragraph{Generated daisy cube.} Compute $\dc(X)$ by downward closure: repeatedly remove one
element at a time from generators, collecting all reachable subsets. Complexity
$O(|\dc(X)|\cdot n)$.

\paragraph{Forbidden-minor construction.} Build $\{0,1,2\}^r\times\{0,1\}^s$, delete the two
grid antipodes in a fixed cube copy, and connect vertices at grid-or-cube distance $1$.

\section{Applications and connections}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Enumeration.} Theorem~\ref{thm:fp} identifies daisy subcubes (for a fixed
embedding) with down-closed families, counted by the Dedekind number $M(n)$ (OEIS A000372:
$2,3,6,20,168,7581,\dots$).
\item \textbf{Chemical graph theory.} Partial cubes model benzenoid graphs; daisy cubes capture
down-closed substructures, and forbidden-minor lists give local membership certificates.
\item \textbf{Concept lattices.} Daisy cubes are precisely the order ideals of the Boolean
lattice with their hypercube metric.
\item \textbf{Median structures.} The meet-gate is a one-sided analogue of the median property;
daisy cubes lie between median graphs and general partial cubes.
\end{itemize}

\section{Discussion and future work}
The verified results---the lattice closure (Theorem~\ref{thm:lattice}), the down-closure
fixed-point characterization (Theorem~\ref{thm:fp}), the meet-on-geodesic identity
(Theorem~\ref{thm:meet}), and the join-failure counterexample (Theorem~\ref{thm:join})---form
the foundation supporting the characterization (Theorem~\ref{thm:main}). The remaining program:

\begin{conjecture}[Meet-closed bottom]
A finite partial cube is a daisy cube iff it embeds isometrically into some $Q_n$ with image
closed under coordinatewise meet and containing $\emptyset$.
\end{conjecture}
\begin{conjecture}[Dedekind enumeration]
The number of daisy subcubes of $Q_n$ (up to coordinate embedding) equals $M(n)$.
\end{conjecture}
\begin{conjecture}[Product closure]
Cartesian products of daisy cubes are daisy cubes, and every daisy cube with a non-peripheral
$\Theta$-class contains a $P_3\,\square\,(\cdot)$ subproduct.
\end{conjecture}
\begin{conjecture}[Minimality via join-failure]
For $r\ge2$, $s\ge1$, $(P_3^{\,r}\,\square\,Q_s)\setminus\{u,v\}$ is a partial cube that is not a
daisy cube, all of whose proper pc-minors are daisy cubes; these are the only minimal
obstructions.
\end{conjecture}

\section*{Appendix: Symbol glossary}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{ll}
\toprule
Symbol & Meaning \\
\midrule
$Q_n$ & $n$-cube: vertices $\PowerSet([n])$, edges at symmetric-difference $1$ \\
$d(A,B)=|A\symdiff B|$ & Hamming distance (\texttt{hdist}) \\

$\square$ & Cartesian product of graphs \\

\end{tabular}

Daisy Cubes: numerical demonstrations of the structural theorems.

Self-contained, dependency-free Python (standard library only).

We model a vertex of the hypercube Q_n as a frozenset of integers drawn from
{0, ..., n-1} (the set of "switches that are up").  The Hamming distance is the
size of the symmetric difference.  A daisy cube is a *down-closed* family of
such vertices.

This script demonstrates, with concrete numbers, every formalized result:

  * hdist / d(A,B) = |A symmetric-difference B|
  * IsDaisy            : down-closedness
  * downClosure / dc(X): smallest daisy cube containing X
  * isDaisy_iff_downClosure_le : fixed-point characterization
  * IsDaisy.inter / .union / .iInter : lattice closure
  * IsDaisy.empty_mem  : nonempty daisy cube contains the origin
  * IsDaisy.inter_mem  : meet closure
  * meet_on_geodesic   : d(A,B) = d(A, A&B) + d(A&B, B)
  * not_join_closed    : {{}, {0}, {1}} is a daisy cube but not join-closed
  * forbidden family   : (P3^r [] Q_s) \\ {u, v}
  * Dedekind link      : #daisy subcubes of Q_n = M(n)
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import combinations, product
from typing import Dict, FrozenSet, Iterable, List, Set, Tuple

Vertex = FrozenSet[int]
Family = Set[Vertex]


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Core hypercube metric
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def hdist(a: Vertex, b: Vertex) -> int:
    """Hamming distance d(A,B) = |A symmetric-difference B|."""
    return len(a ^ b)


def all_vertices(n: int) -> List[Vertex]:
    """All 2^n vertices of Q_n as frozensets of {0,...,n-1}."""
    verts: List[Vertex] = []
    for k in range(n + 1):
        for combo in combinations(range(n), k):
            verts.append(frozenset(combo))
    return verts


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Daisy cubes and the down-closure operator
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def is_daisy(family: Iterable[Vertex]) -> bool:
    """IsDaisy: a family is down-closed iff every subset of a member is a member."""
    fam: Family = set(family)
    for a in fam:
        elems = sorted(a)
        # It suffices to check single-element removals (Theorem: fixed-point test),
        # but we verify the full down-set here for transparency.
        for k in range(len(elems) + 1):
            for combo in combinations(elems, k):
                if frozenset(combo) not in fam:
                    return False
    return True


def down_closure(generators: Iterable[Vertex]) -> Family:
    """dc(X): the smallest daisy cube containing X (union of intervals [0, C])."""
    closure: Family = set()
    frontier: List[Vertex] = list(generators)
    while frontier:
        a = frontier.pop()
        if a in closure:
            continue
        closure.add(a)
        for x in a:
            frontier.append(a - {x})
    return closure


def fixed_point_test(family: Iterable[Vertex]) -> bool:
    """isDaisy_iff_downClosure_le: D is a daisy cube iff dc(D) == D."""
    fam: Family = set(family)
    return down_closure(fam) == fam


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Lattice closure
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def daisy_inter(d1: Family, d2: Family) -> Family:
    """IsDaisy.inter: intersection of daisy cubes is a daisy cube."""
    return d1 & d2


def daisy_union(d1: Family, d2: Family) -> Family:
    """IsDaisy.union: union of daisy cubes is a daisy cube."""
    return d1 | d2


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# The forbidden family  (P3^r [] Q_s) \ {u, v}
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
GridVertex = Tuple[Tuple[int, ...], Tuple[int, ...]]  # (P3^r coords, Q_s coords)


def forbidden_family(r: int, s: int) -> Tuple[List[GridVertex], List[Tuple[GridVertex, GridVertex]]]:
    """
    Construct G_{r,s} = (P3^r [] Q_s) \\ {u, v}.

    P3^r vertices are {0,1,2}^r; Q_s vertices are {0,1}^s.  We delete the two
    antipodal P3^r-corners (all-0 and all-2) in the same Q_s copy (w = all-0).
    Returns (vertices, edges).
    """
    grid = list(product(range(3), repeat=r))
    cube = list(product(range(2), repeat=s))
    w0 = tuple([0] * s)
    u = (tuple([0] * r), w0)
    v = (tuple([2] * r), w0)
    removed = {u, v}

    verts: List[GridVertex] = [(g, w) for g in grid for w in cube if (g, w) not in removed]
    vset = set(verts)

    def adjacent(p: GridVertex, q: GridVertex) -> bool:
        (g1, w1), (g2, w2) = p, q
        if w1 == w2:
            diff = [i for i in range(r) if g1[i] != g2[i]]
            return len(diff) == 1 and abs(g1[diff[0]] - g2[diff[0]]) == 1
        if g1 == g2:
            return sum(1 for i in range(s) if w1[i] != w2[i]) == 1
        return False

    edges: List[Tuple[GridVertex, GridVertex]] = []
    for p, q in combinations(verts, 2):
        if adjacent(p, q) and p in vset and q in vset:
            edges.append((p, q))
    return verts, edges


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Dedekind connection: count daisy subcubes of Q_n (down-closed families)
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def count_daisy_subcubes(n: int) -> int:
    """
    Number of daisy cubes inside Q_n for a fixed coordinate embedding
    = number of down-closed families = Dedekind number M(n)
    (OEIS A000372: 2, 3, 6, 20, 168, ...).
    Brute force; feasible for n <= 3 (n=4 already explores 2^16 subsets).
    """
    verts = all_vertices(n)
    count = 0
    for mask in range(1 << len(verts)):
        family = {verts[i] for i in range(len(verts)) if (mask >> i) & 1}
        if is_daisy(family):
            count += 1
    return count


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Demonstrations
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def demo_distance_and_meet() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("meet_on_geodesic:  d(A,B) = d(A, A&B) + d(A&B, B)")
    print("=" * 70)
    examples: List[Tuple[Vertex, Vertex]] = [
        (frozenset({0, 1, 2}), frozenset({2, 3})),
        (frozenset({0, 1, 3, 4}), frozenset({1, 4, 5})),
        (frozenset(), frozenset({0, 1, 2})),
    ]
    for a, b in examples:
        m = a & b
        lhs = hdist(a, b)
        rhs = hdist(a, m) + hdist(m, b)
        print(f"  A={set(a)}, B={set(b)}, A&B={set(m)}: "
              f"d(A,B)={lhs}  ==  {hdist(a, m)}+{hdist(m, b)}={rhs}  -> {lhs == rhs}")
    print()


def demo_down_closure() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("down_closure & fixed-point characterization")
    print("=" * 70)
    gens: Family = {frozenset({0, 1}), frozenset({1, 2})}
    dc = down_closure(gens)
    print("  generators X =", sorted(map(sorted, gens)))
    print("  dc(X)        =", sorted(map(sorted, dc)))
    print("  is_daisy(dc(X))            :", is_daisy(dc))
    print("  fixed_point_test(dc(X))    :", fixed_point_test(dc))
    not_daisy = {frozenset({0, 1}), frozenset({1, 2})}
    print("  is_daisy(X) (X not closed) :", is_daisy(not_daisy))
    print()


def demo_lattice() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("Lattice closure: intersection and union stay daisy cubes")
    print("=" * 70)
    d1 = down_closure({frozenset({0, 1})})
    d2 = down_closure({frozenset({1, 2})})
    inter = daisy_inter(d1, d2)
    union = daisy_union(d1, d2)
    print("  d1 = dc({0,1}),  d2 = dc({1,2})")
    print("  is_daisy(d1 & d2):", is_daisy(inter), " | is_daisy(d1 | d2):", is_daisy(union))
    print("  origin in nonempty daisy cube d1:", frozenset() in d1, "(empty_mem)")
    print()


def demo_join_failure() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("not_join_closed: a daisy cube need not contain joins")
    print("=" * 70)
    d: Family = {frozenset(), frozenset({0}), frozenset({1})}  # the path P3
    print("  D = {{}, {0}, {1}}  is_daisy:", is_daisy(d))
    join = frozenset({0}) | frozenset({1})
    print("  {0} in D:", frozenset({0}) in d, " {1} in D:", frozenset({1}) in d)
    print("  join {0,1} in D:", join in d, " -> daisy cubes are NOT join-closed")
    # but meet IS present:
    meet = frozenset({0}) & frozenset({1})
    print("  meet {} in D:", meet in d, "  (IsDaisy.inter_mem holds)")
    print()


def demo_forbidden_family() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("Forbidden family  G_{r,s} = (P3^r [] Q_s) \\ {u, v}")
    print("=" * 70)
    for r, s in [(2, 1), (2, 2), (3, 1)]:
        verts, edges = forbidden_family(r, s)
        full = 3 ** r * 2 ** s
        print(f"  r={r}, s={s}: |V(P3^r [] Q_s)|={full}, "
              f"after deleting 2 antipodes |V|={len(verts)}, |E|={len(edges)}")
    print()


def demo_dedekind() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("Dedekind link: #daisy subcubes of Q_n = M(n) (A000372)")
    print("=" * 70)
    known = {0: 2, 1: 3, 2: 6, 3: 20}
    for n in range(0, 4):
        c = count_daisy_subcubes(n)
        print(f"  n={n}: counted={c}, Dedekind M({n})={known[n]}, match={c == known[n]}")
    print()


def main() -> None:
    demo_distance_and_meet()
    demo_down_closure()
    demo_lattice()
    demo_join_failure()
    demo_forbidden_family()
    demo_dedekind()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

    verts: List[GridVertex] = [(g, w) for g in grid for w in cube

        (g1, w1), (g2, w2) = p, q
        if w1 == w2:

  "future_directions": "# Future Directions — Forbidden pc-minors for Daisy Cubes

Derived from this cycle's formalized findings:
- `daisy_isometric` — daisy cubes are partial cubes (isometric subgraphs of `Q_n`);
- `meet_on_geodesic` / `IsDaisy.inter_mem` — daisy cubes are meet-closed and the meet is a geodesic gate;
- `not_join_closed` — daisy cubes are *not* join-closed (the meet/join asymmetry);
- `isDaisy_iff_downClosure_le` — daisy cubes are exactly the fixed points of the down-closure
  (interval-union-to-origin) operator.

Each conjecture below is stated so that it can be falsified by a single counterexample or settled by
a formal proof in the present `DaisyCubes` framework.

## Conjecture 1 — Meet-closed bottom characterization
A finite partial cube `G` is a daisy cube **iff** it has an isometric embedding into some `Q_n` whose
image is closed under coordinatewise meet and contains the all-zero vertex `∅`.
- **The key insight is** that `meet_on_geodesic` shows the meet always lies on a geodesic, so
  "down-closed" is equivalent to "meet-closed with a global bottom" — the order condition is forced
  by the metric.
- **Why now?** We have just formalized both `IsDaisy.inter_mem` (meet closure) and the geodesic
  identity, which are exactly the two halves the equivalence needs.

## Conjecture 2 — Dedekind enumeration
The number of daisy cubes that are isometric subgraphs of `Q_n` (up to fixing the coordinate
embedding) equals the Dedekind number `M(n)` = number of down-sets of the Boolean lattice
(OEIS A000372: 2, 3, 6, 20, 168, 7581, …).
- **The key insight is** that `isDaisy_iff_downClosure_le` makes "daisy cube" literally synonymous
  with "down-closed family", and down-closed families are counted by Dedekind numbers.
- **Why now?** The fixed-point characterization removes all graph-theoretic overhead and turns the
  count into a pure lattice-enumeration question.

## Conjecture 3 — Product closure of daisy cubes
If `D₁ ⊆ Q_a` and `D₂ ⊆ Q_b` are daisy cubes, then their Cartesian product `D₁ □ D₂ ⊆ Q_{a+b}` is a
daisy cube; conversely every daisy cube containing a non-peripheral Θ-class contains a subproduct of
the form `P₃ □ (·)`.
- **The key insight is** that down-closure is preserved by products of Boolean lattices, so the

    "demo": """"
Daisy Cubes: numerical demonstrations of the structural theorems.

Self-contained, dependency-free Python (standard library only).

We model a vertex of the hypercube Q_n as a frozenset of integers drawn from
{0, ..., n-1} (the set of "switches that are up").  The Hamming distance is the
size of the symmetric difference.  A daisy cube is a *down-closed* family of
such vertices.

This script demonstrates, with concrete numbers, every formalized result:

  * hdist / d(A,B) = |A symmetric-difference B|
  * IsDaisy            : down-closedness
  * downClosure / dc(X): smallest daisy cube containing X
  * isDaisy_iff_downClosure_le : fixed-point characterization
  * IsDaisy.inter / .union / .iInter : lattice closure
  * IsDaisy.empty_mem  : nonempty daisy cube contains the origin
  * IsDaisy.inter_mem  : meet closure
  * meet_on_geodesic   : d(A,B) = d(A, A&B) + d(A&B, B)
  * not_join_closed    : {{}, {0}, {1}} is a daisy cube but not join-closed
  * forbidden family   : (P3^r [] Q_s) \\ {u, v}
  * Dedekind link      : #daisy subcubes of Q_n = M(n)
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import combinations, product
from typing import Dict, FrozenSet, Iterable, List, Set, Tuple

Vertex = FrozenSet[int]
Family = Set[Vertex]


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Core hypercube metric
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def hdist(a: Vertex, b: Vertex) -> int:
    """Hamming distance d(A,B) = |A symmetric-difference B|."""
    return len(a ^ b)


def all_vertices(n: int) -> List[Vertex]:
    """All 2^n vertices of Q_n as frozensets of {0,...,n-1}."""
    verts: List[Vertex] = []
    for k in range(n + 1):
        for combo in combinations(range(n), k):
            verts.append(frozenset(combo))
    return verts


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Daisy cubes and the down-closure operator
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def is_daisy(family: Iterable[Vertex]) -> bool:
    """IsDaisy: a family is down-closed iff every subset of a member is a member."""
    fam: Family = set(family)
    for a in fam:
        elems = sorted(a)
        # It suffices to check single-element removals (Theorem: fixed-point test),
        # but we verify the full down-set here for transparency.
        for k in range(len(elems) + 1):
            for combo in combinations(elems, k):
                if frozenset(combo) not in fam:
                    return False
    return True


def down_closure(generators: Iterable[Vertex]) -> Family:
    """dc(X): the smallest daisy cube containing X (union of intervals [0, C])."""
    closure: Family = set()
    frontier: List[Vertex] = list(generators)
    while frontier:
        a = frontier.pop()
        if a in closure:
            continue
        closure.add(a)
        for x in a:
            frontier.append(a - {x})
    return closure


def fixed_point_test(family: Iterable[Vertex]) -> bool:
    """isDaisy_iff_downClosure_le: D is a daisy cube iff dc(D) == D."""
    fam: Family = set(family)
    return down_closure(fam) == fam


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Lattice closure
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def daisy_inter(d1: Family, d2: Family) -> Family:
    """IsDaisy.inter: intersection of daisy cubes is a daisy cube."""
    return d1 & d2


def daisy_union(d1: Family, d2: Family) -> Family:
    """IsDaisy.union: union of daisy cubes is a daisy cube."""
    return d1 | d2


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# The forbidden family  (P3^r [] Q_s) \ {u, v}
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
GridVertex = Tuple[Tuple[int, ...], Tuple[int, ...]]  # (P3^r coords, Q_s coords)


def forbidden_family(r: int, s: int) -> Tuple[List[GridVertex], List[Tuple[GridVertex, GridVertex]]]:
    """
    Construct G_{r,s} = (P3^r [] Q_s) \\ {u, v}.

    P3^r vertices are {0,1,2}^r; Q_s vertices are {0,1}^s.  We delete the two
    antipodal P3^r-corners (all-0 and all-2) in the same Q_s copy (w = all-0).
    Returns (vertices, edges).
    """
    grid = list(product(range(3), repeat=r))
    cube = list(product(range(2), repeat=s))
    w0 = tuple([0] * s)
    u = (tuple([0] * r), w0)
    v = (tuple([2] * r), w0)
    removed = {u, v}

    verts: List[GridVertex] = [(g, w) for g in grid for w in cube if (g, w) not in removed]
    vset = set(verts)

    def adjacent(p: GridVertex, q: GridVertex) -> bool:
        (g1, w1), (g2, w2) = p, q
        if w1 == w2:
            diff = [i for i in range(r) if g1[i] != g2[i]]
            return len(diff) == 1 and abs(g1[diff[0]] - g2[diff[0]]) == 1
        if g1 == g2:
            return sum(1 for i in range(s) if w1[i] != w2[i]) == 1
        return False

    edges: List[Tuple[GridVertex, GridVertex]] = []
    for p, q in combinations(verts, 2):
        if adjacent(p, q) and p in vset and q in vset:
            edges.append((p, q))
    return verts, edges


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Dedekind connection: count daisy subcubes of Q_n (down-closed families)
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def count_daisy_subcubes(n: int) -> int:
    """
    Number of daisy cubes inside Q_n for a fixed coordinate embedding
    = number of down-closed families = Dedekind number M(n)
    (OEIS A000372: 2, 3, 6, 20, 168, ...).
    Brute force; feasible for n <= 3 (n=4 already explores 2^16 subsets).
    """
    verts = all_vertices(n)
    count = 0
    for mask in range(1 << len(verts)):
        family = {verts[i] for i in range(len(verts)) if (mask >> i) & 1}
        if is_daisy(family):
            count += 1
    return count


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# Demonstrations
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def demo_distance_and_meet() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("meet_on_geodesic:  d(A,B) = d(A, A&B) + d(A&B, B)")
    print("=" * 70)
    examples: List[Tuple[Vertex, Vertex]] = [
        (frozenset({0, 1, 2}), frozenset({2, 3})),
        (frozenset({0, 1, 3, 4}), frozenset({1, 4, 5})),
        (frozenset(), frozenset({0, 1, 2})),
    ]
    for a, b in examples:
        m = a & b
        lhs = hdist(a, b)
        rhs = hdist(a, m) + hdist(m, b)
        print(f"  A={set(a)}, B={set(b)}, A&B={set(m)}: "
              f"d(A,B)={lhs}  ==  {hdist(a, m)}+{hdist(m, b)}={rhs}  -> {lhs == rhs}")
    print()


def demo_down_closure() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("down_closure & fixed-point characterization")
    print("=" * 70)
    gens: Family = {frozenset({0, 1}), frozenset({1, 2})}
    dc = down_closure(gens)
    print("  generators X =", sorted(map(sorted, gens)))
    print("  dc(X)        =", sorted(map(sorted, dc)))
    print("  is_daisy(dc(X))            :", is_daisy(dc))
    print("  fixed_point_test(dc(X))    :", fixed_point_test(dc))
    not_daisy = {frozenset({0, 1}), frozenset({1, 2})}
    print("  is_daisy(X) (X not closed) :", is_daisy(not_daisy))
    print()


def demo_lattice() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("Lattice closure: intersection and union stay daisy cubes")
    print("=" * 70)
    d1 = down_closure({frozenset({0, 1})})
    d2 = down_closure({frozenset({1, 2})})
    inter = daisy_inter(d1, d2)
    union = daisy_union(d1, d2)
    print("  d1 = dc({0,1}),  d2 = dc({1,2})")
    print("  is_daisy(d1 & d2):", is_daisy(inter), " | is_daisy(d1 | d2):", is_daisy(union))
    print("  origin in nonempty daisy cube d1:", frozenset() in d1, "(empty_mem)")
    print()


def demo_join_failure() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("not_join_closed: a daisy cube need not contain joins")
    print("=" * 70)
    d: Family = {frozenset(), frozenset({0}), frozenset({1})}  # the path P3
    print("  D = {{}, {0}, {1}}  is_daisy:", is_daisy(d))
    join = frozenset({0}) | frozenset({1})
    print("  {0} in D:", frozenset({0}) in d, " {1} in D:", frozenset({1}) in d)
    print("  join {0,1} in D:", join in d, " -> daisy cubes are NOT join-closed")
    # but meet IS present:
    meet = frozenset({0}) & frozenset({1})
    print("  meet {} in D:", meet in d, "  (IsDaisy.inter_mem holds)")
    print()


def demo_forbidden_family() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("Forbidden family  G_{r,s} = (P3^r [] Q_s) \\ {u, v}")
    print("=" * 70)
    for r, s in [(2, 1), (2, 2), (3, 1)]:
        verts, edges = forbidden_family(r, s)
        full = 3 ** r * 2 ** s
        print(f"  r={r}, s={s}: |V(P3^r [] Q_s)|={full}, "
              f"after deleting 2 antipodes |V|={len(verts)}, |E|={len(edges)}")
    print()


def demo_dedekind() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("Dedekind link: #daisy subcubes of Q_n = M(n) (A000372)")
    print("=" * 70)
    known = {0: 2, 1: 3, 2: 6, 3: 20}
    for n in range(0, 4):
        c = count_daisy_subcubes(n)
        print(f"  n={n}: counted={c}, Dedekind M({n})={known[n]}, match={c == known[n]}")
    print()


def main() -> None:
    demo_distance_and_meet()
    demo_down_closure()
    demo_lattice()
    demo_join_failure()
    demo_forbidden_family()
    demo_dedekind()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The single combinatorial fact driving everything is

open Finset
open scoped symmDiff

namespace DeltaMatroid

variable {α : Type*} [DecidableEq α]

/-! ### The parity engine -/

/-- **Parity engine.**  A twist by `A` shifts the size parity by `|A|`:
`|F ∆ A| ≡ |F| + |A|  (mod 2)`. -/
theorem card_symmDiff_mod_two (F A : Finset α) :
    (F ∆ A).card % 2 = (F.card + A.card) % 2 := by
  have hdef : (F ∆ A) = (F \ A) ∪ (A \ F) := symmDiff_def F A
  have hdisj : Disjoint (F \ A) (A \ F) := by
    apply Finset.disjoint_left.mpr; intro x hx hx2
    simp only [Finset.mem_sdiff] at hx hx2; exact hx2.2 hx.1
  have hc : (F ∆ A).card = (F \ A).card + (A \ F).card := by
    rw [hdef, Finset.card_union_of_disjoint hdisj]
  have h1 : (F \ A).card + (F ∩ A).card = F.card := by
    rw [Finset.card_sdiff_add_card_inter]
  have h2 : (A \ F).card + (A ∩ F).card = A.card := by
    rw [Finset.card_sdiff_add_card_inter]
  rw [Finset.inter_comm A F] at h2
  omega

/-! ### Parity-restricted twist domains and the generalized partial polynomial -/

/-- The set of twists `A ⊆ E` with `|A|` even. -/
def evenTwists (E : Finset α) : Finset (Finset α) :=
  E.powerset.filter (fun A => A.card % 2 = 0)

/-- The set of twists `A ⊆ E` with `|A|` odd. -/
def oddTwists (E : Finset α) : Finset (Finset α) :=
  E.powerset.filter (fun A => A.card % 2 = 1)

/-- The generalized partial-twuality coefficient over an arbitrary twist domain `S`:
the number of twists `A ∈ S` whose twisted feasible set `F ∆ A` has size `k`. -/
def tCoeff (S : Finset (Finset α)) (F : Finset α) (k : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  (S.filter (fun A => (F ∆ A).card = k)).card

/-- An integer-coefficient sequence is an *even polynomial* if every nonzero coefficient
sits at an even degree. -/
def IsEvenPoly (c : ℕ → ℕ) : Prop := ∀ k, 0 < c k → Even k

/-- An integer-coefficient sequence is an *odd polynomial* if every nonzero coefficient
sits at an odd degree. -/
def IsOddPoly (c : ℕ → ℕ) : Prop := ∀ k, 0 < c k → Odd k

/-- *Even-interpolating up to `hi`*: among even degrees the support is exactly `[0, hi]`
(no gaps between even degrees). -/
def EvenInterp (hi : ℕ) (c : ℕ → ℕ) : Prop := ∀ k, Even k → (0 < c k ↔ k ≤ hi)

/-- *Odd-interpolating up to `hi`*: among odd degrees the support is exactly `[1, hi]`
(no gaps between odd degrees). -/
def OddInterp (hi : ℕ) (c : ℕ → ℕ) : Prop := ∀ k, Odd k → (0 < c k ↔ k ≤ hi)

/-! ### Support of parity-restricted partial polynomials -/

/-
**Even-domain support (parity-interpolation).**  Over even twists the support is
*exactly* the step-2 progression `{k ≤ |E| : k ≡ |F| (mod 2)}`: every degree of the
right parity below `|E|` is hit, with no gaps.
-/
theorem tCoeff_even_pos_iff {E F : Finset α} (hF : F ⊆ E) (k : ℕ) :
    0 < tCoeff (evenTwists E) F k ↔ (k % 2 = F.card % 2 ∧ k ≤ E.card) := by
  constructor;
  · intro hk;
    obtain ⟨ A, hA ⟩ := Finset.card_pos.mp hk;
    have := card_symmDiff_mod_two F A; simp_all +decide [ evenTwists ] ;
    exact ⟨ by omega, hA.2 ▸ Finset.card_le_card ( symmDiff_subset_of_subset hF hA.1.1 ) ⟩;
  · intro hk
    obtain ⟨B, hB⟩ : ∃ B ⊆ E, B.card = k ∧ (F.card + B.card) % 2 = 0 := by
      exact Exists.elim ( Finset.exists_subset_card_eq hk.2 ) fun B hB => ⟨ B, hB.1, hB.2, by omega ⟩;
    refine' Finset.card_pos.mpr ⟨ F ∆ B, _ ⟩ ; simp_all +decide [ evenTwists ];
    exact ⟨ symmDiff_subset_of_subset hF hB.1, by rw [ card_symmDiff_mod_two ] ; aesop ⟩

/-
**Odd-domain support (parity-interpolation).**  Over odd twists the support is
*exactly* the opposite step-2 progression `{k ≤ |E| : k ≡ |F| + 1 (mod 2)}`.
-/
theorem tCoeff_odd_pos_iff {E F : Finset α} (hF : F ⊆ E) (k : ℕ) :
    0 < tCoeff (oddTwists E) F k ↔ (k % 2 = (F.card + 1) % 2 ∧ k ≤ E.card) := by
  constructor;
  · intro hk_pos
    obtain ⟨A, hA₁, hA₂⟩ : ∃ A ∈ oddTwists E, (F ∆ A).card = k := by
      exact Exists.elim ( Finset.card_pos.mp hk_pos ) fun x hx => ⟨ x, Finset.mem_filter.mp hx |>.1, Finset.mem_filter.mp hx |>.2 ⟩;
    have := card_symmDiff_mod_two F A; simp_all +decide [ Nat.add_mod, oddTwists ] ;
    exact hA₂ ▸ Finset.card_le_card ( symmDiff_subset_of_subset hF hA₁.1 );
  · intro hk
    obtain ⟨B, hB⟩ : ∃ B ⊆ E, B.card = k := by
      exact Finset.exists_subset_card_eq hk.2;
    refine' Finset.card_pos.mpr ⟨ F ∆ B, _ ⟩;
    simp_all +decide [ Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_powerset, DeltaMatroid.oddTwists ];
    exact ⟨ DeltaMatroid.symmDiff_subset_of_subset hF hB.1, by rw [ DeltaMatroid.card_symmDiff_mod_two ] ; omega ⟩

/-! ### Pure parity of the restricted polynomials -/

/-
Over even twists with an even base feasible set, the partial polynomial is even.
-/
theorem parityTwist_evenF_isEven {E F : Finset α} (hF : F ⊆ E) (hp : Even F.card) :
    IsEvenPoly (tCoeff (evenTwists E) F) := by
  intro k hk; have := tCoeff_even_pos_iff hF k; simp_all +decide [ Nat.even_iff ] ;

/-
Over even twists with an odd base feasible set, the partial polynomial is odd.
-/
theorem parityTwist_oddF_isOdd {E F : Finset α} (hF : F ⊆ E) (hp : Odd F.card) :
    IsOddPoly (tCoeff (evenTwists E) F) := by
  intro k hk;
  exact Nat.odd_iff.mpr ( by have := tCoeff_even_pos_iff hF k; have := Nat.odd_iff.mp hp; aesop )

/-
Over odd twists with an even base feasible set, the partial polynomial is odd.
-/
theorem parityTwist_evenF_oddTwists_isOdd {E F : Finset α} (hF : F ⊆ E) (hp : Even F.card) :
    IsOddPoly (tCoeff (oddTwists E) F) := by
  intro k hk; specialize hk; have := tCoeff_odd_pos_iff hF k; simp_all +decide [ Nat.even_iff ] ;
  exact Nat.odd_iff.mpr ( by omega )

/-
Over odd twists with an odd base feasible set, the partial polynomial is even.
-/
theorem parityTwist_oddF_oddTwists_isEven {E F : Finset α} (hF : F ⊆ E) (hp : Odd F.card) :
    IsEvenPoly (tCoeff (oddTwists E) F) := by
  intro k hk; specialize hk; have := tCoeff_odd_pos_iff hF k; simp_all +decide [ Nat.even_iff, Nat.odd_iff ] ;
  omega

/-! ### Full-domain double interpolation -/

/-- The full-domain coefficient agrees with the catalog `ptCoeff`. -/
theorem tCoeff_powerset (E F : Finset α) (k : ℕ) :
    tCoeff E.powerset F k = ptCoeff E F k := rfl

/-
**Both even- and odd-interpolating.**  Over all twists the partial polynomial hits
every degree in `[0, |E|]`, hence is simultaneously even-interpolating and
odd-interpolating.
-/
theorem tCoeff_full_both_interp {E F : Finset α} (hF : F ⊆ E) :
    EvenInterp E.card (tCoeff E.powerset F) ∧ OddInterp E.card (tCoeff E.powerset F) := by
  constructor; all_goals intro k hk; rw [ tCoeff_powerset ] ; exact ( ptCoeff_pos_iff hF k ) ;

/-! ### The twuality operators and the master trichotomy -/

/-- The five nontrivial twuality operators of the duality–Petriality group `S₃`. -/
inductive Twuality
  | star          -- `∗`     (reflection)
  | petrie        -- `×`     (reflection)
  | starPetrie    -- `∗×`    (rotation)
  | petrieStar    -- `×∗`    (rotation)
  | starPetrieStar-- `∗×∗`   (reflection)
deriving DecidableEq, Repr

/-- Twist domain realising the partial-`•` polynomial.  Reflections (`∗, ×, ∗×∗`) act
within a fixed `|A|`-parity sector; rotations (`∗×, ×∗`) act on the full domain. -/
def Twuality.domain (op : Twuality) (E : Finset α) : Finset (Finset α) :=
  match op with
  | .star           => evenTwists E
  | .petrie         => oddTwists E
  | .starPetrieStar => evenTwists E
  | .starPetrie     => E.powerset
  | .petrieStar     => E.powerset

/-- The partial-`•` polynomial coefficient of a feasible set `F` over a twuality
operator `op`. -/
def partialTwuality (op : Twuality) (E F : Finset α) (k : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  tCoeff (op.domain E) F k

/-
**Master trichotomy.**  For every nontrivial twuality operator `op` and every
feasible set `F ⊆ E`, the partial-`op` polynomial is *even*, *odd*, or *both
even-interpolating and odd-interpolating*.
-/
theorem partialTwuality_trichotomy (op : Twuality) {E F : Finset α} (hF : F ⊆ E) :
    IsEvenPoly (partialTwuality op E F)
    ∨ IsOddPoly (partialTwuality op E F)
    ∨ (EvenInterp E.card (partialTwuality op E F)
        ∧ OddInterp E.card (partialTwuality op E F)) := by
  rcases op with ( _ | _ | _ | _ | _ );
  · exact Or.imp ( parityTwist_evenF_isEven hF ) ( Or.inl ∘ parityTwist_oddF_isOdd hF ) ( Nat.even_or_odd F.card );
  · cases' em ( Even F.card ) with hp hp <;> simp_all +decide [ IsEvenPoly, IsOddPoly ];
    · exact Or.inr <| Or.inl <| parityTwist_evenF_oddTwists_isOdd hF hp;
    · exact Or.inl ( parityTwist_oddF_oddTwists_isEven hF hp );
  · exact Or.inr <| Or.inr <| by simpa [ partialTwuality, Twuality.domain ] using tCoeff_full_both_interp hF;
  · exact Or.inr <| Or.inr <| tCoeff_full_both_interp hF;
  · cases' Nat.even_or_odd F.card with hp hp;
    · exact Or.inl ( parityTwist_evenF_isEven hF hp );
    · exact Or.inr <| Or.inl <| parityTwist_oddF_isOdd hF hp

/-
Non-vacuity: for nonempty `E` the rotation (full-domain) partial polynomial really
does have both an even and an odd nonzero coefficient, so the "both-interpolating"
disjunct is genuine, never a degenerate monomial.
-/
theorem partialTwuality_support_nontrivial {E F : Finset α} (hF : F ⊆ E) (hne : E.Nonempty) :
    0 < partialTwuality .starPetrie E F 0
      ∧ 0 < partialTwuality .starPetrie E F E.card
      ∧ (0 : ℕ) ≠ E.card := by
  refine ⟨?_, ?_, ?_⟩
  · show 0 < ptCoeff E F 0
    exact (ptCoeff_pos_iff hF 0).mpr (Nat.zero_le _)
  · show 0 < ptCoeff E F E.card
    exact (ptCoeff_pos_iff hF E.card).mpr (le_refl _)
  · have := Finset.card_pos.mpr hne; omega

end DeltaMatroid
